extracted.intended_audience: content creators, journalists, science communicators, marketers, and researchers interested in what makes online content shareable
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what characteristics of online articles, summaries, videos, and posts increase their likelihood of being widely shared (virality). Focuses on emotional, practical, and framing features that boost shareability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicit an emotional reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that elicits an emotional reaction tends to be more widely shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall, content that elicits emotion (vs. none) increases shareability. The authors' analyses of New York Times articles and lab experiments both show that greater emotionality raises the likelihood a piece will appear on the most-e-mailed list or be reported as likely to be shared. Make messages emotional rather than emotionally flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive valence increases sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories stimulating positive emotions are more widely shared than those eliciting negative feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, make the message positive — positive emotions like awe or wonder boost shareability more than negative emotions. Example contrasts from the NYT dataset include a very positive article ('Wide-Eyed New Arrivals Falling in Love with the City') vs. very negative ('Germany: Baby Polar Bear’s Feeder Dies').

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional arousal / activation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that produces greater emotional arousal (making your heart race) is more likely to go viral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activating emotions (those that increase physiological arousal) — e.g., awe, amusement, anger, anxiety — increase sharing. Deactivating emotions such as sadness reduce the likelihood of sharing. Thus, aim for emotions that are activating rather than merely valenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific high-activation emotions help (awe, amusement, anger, anxiety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions like awe, amusement and anger are particularly effective at increasing reported sharing likelihood; anger more than sadness because it produces greater arousal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes that positive activating emotions such as awe and wonder increase sharing, and that anger-inducing content is more likely to be shared than sadness-inducing content. In experiments, high- vs low-emotion versions of the same stories produced higher reported sharing when they induced activating emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value / usefulness increases sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that is practically useful or offers practical value is more likely to be widely shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the analyses, usefulness was controlled for and found to be associated with higher shareability. In the study of scientist summaries, describing research to enhance its usefulness increased lay readers' reported willingness to share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interestingness and surprise boost shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: Content judged more interesting or more surprising is more likely to be shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors controlled for how interesting and surprising readers found items; higher ratings on these dimensions correlated with increased chances of making the most-e-mailed list. Framing that highlights novelty or surprising findings can therefore help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframe the same content to increase emotionality, positivity, usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The same underlying content can be described differently to raise its emotionality, positivity, and usefulness, thereby increasing its shareability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laboratory experiments showed participants were more likely to report sharing when the identical story was presented in higher-emotion or more positive/useful versions. Practical implication: craft headlines and summaries to emphasize activating emotion, positivity, and practical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting contagious content may outperform influencer-targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating emotionally engaging, useful content may be more effective than strategies that focus on targeting 'influentials' or opinion leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors suggest that improving the intrinsic contagiousness of content could provide more reliable viral reach than relying primarily on identifying and targeting high-status individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for placement and non-content factors when evaluating shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-content factors — e.g., where a story is featured, time spent in prominent positions on a homepage, release timing, author fame, writing complexity, author gender, length, and topic — affect sharing and should be controlled for in analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In their NYT study they controlled for these variables when testing hypotheses about valence and emotionality. Practical implication for producers and analysts: prominence, timing, and author-related characteristics influence observed sharing independently of content features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and concrete emotional hooks in science communication
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing scientific findings for lay audiences, emphasizing emotionality, positivity, and usefulness increases the likelihood readers will share the summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the authors' second study, subtle differences in how co-authors described the same research influenced shareability; phrasing that enhanced emotionality, positivity, and usefulness led to higher reported sharing among lay participants. For scientists writing press releases or summaries: frame discoveries to highlight awe, usefulness, or relevance while remaining accurate.
